parts.label: a
parts.body: Find the value of the car after $4$ years, correct to the nearest dollar.
parts.solution: Losing $15\%$ each year multiplies the value by $0.85$ annually, so after $4$ years$$V = 24000(0.85)^{4} = 24000(0.52200625) = 12528.15.$$ Carrying the unrounded power through gives $12528.15$, so to the nearest dollar the car is worth $\$12{,}528$.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find the first year at the end of which the value has fallen below $\$6{,}000$.
parts.solution: The condition is$$24000(0.85)^{n} < 6000 \;\Rightarrow\; (0.85)^{n} < \frac{1}{4}.$$ Taking natural logarithms and remembering that $\ln 0.85$ is NEGATIVE, so the inequality reverses,$$n > \frac{\ln 0.25}{\ln 0.85} = 8.5265\ldots$$ The first whole year that satisfies this is $n = 9$. Checking: after $8$ years the value is $\$6{,}199$ and after $9$ years it is $\$5{,}269$.

questions.contextIntro: A car is bought for $\$24{,}000$. Its value falls by $15\%$ of its value at the start of each year.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Find the number of fish at the moment of stocking.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find the number of fish after $5$ years, giving your answer to the nearest whole fish.
parts.solution: Substituting $t = 5$ makes the exponent $-0.4(5) = -2$:$$P(5) = \frac{5000}{1 + 9\mathrm{e}^{-2}} = \frac{5000}{1 + 9(0.135335\ldots)} = \frac{5000}{2.21802\ldots} = 2254.2\ldots$$ To the nearest whole fish the population is $2254$.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Find the time at which the population reaches $2500$ fish, correct to three significant figures.
parts.solution: Set the model equal to $2500$:$$\frac{5000}{1 + 9\mathrm{e}^{-0.4t}} = 2500 \;\Rightarrow\; 1 + 9\mathrm{e}^{-0.4t} = 2.$$ Hence $\mathrm{e}^{-0.4t} = \dfrac{1}{9}$, and taking logarithms,$$-0.4t = -\ln 9 \;\Rightarrow\; t = \frac{\ln 9}{0.4} = 5.49306\ldots$$ So $t = 5.49$ years. Note $2500$ is exactly half the ceiling of $5000$ — the model's point of fastest growth.

questions.contextIntro: The number of fish in a lake $t$ years after stocking is modelled by $$P(t) = \frac{5000}{1 + 9\mathrm{e}^{-0.4t}}, \quad t \ge 0.$$

parts.label: a
parts.body: Find the two possible sizes of the angle at $C$, each correct to three significant figures.
parts.solution: Pair each side with the angle opposite it. The side $AB = 9$ faces $C$ and $BC = 7$ faces $A$, so$$\frac{\sin C}{9} = \frac{\sin 35^\circ}{7} \;\Rightarrow\; \sin C = \frac{9\sin 35^\circ}{7} = 0.737455\ldots$$ The inverse sine gives $C = 47.5151\ldots^\circ$, but the sine of an obtuse angle is equally positive, so$$C = 180^\circ - 47.5151^\circ = 132.4849\ldots^\circ$$ is a second candidate. To three significant figures the two possibilities are $47.6^\circ$ and $132^\circ$.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Explain why both of these values give a valid triangle here.

markscheme.note: check that the three angles can still sum to $180^\circ$ in each case
each leaves a positive angle at $B$, so both triangles exist

parts.answer: both leave a positive angle at $B$, so two triangles fit the data
parts.solution: An ambiguous case is only genuinely ambiguous if BOTH candidates leave room for a third angle. With $A = 35^\circ$:$$C = 47.5151^\circ \;\Rightarrow\; B = 180 - 35 - 47.5151 = 97.48^\circ,$$$$C = 132.4849^\circ \;\Rightarrow\; B = 180 - 35 - 132.4849 = 12.52^\circ.$$ Both values of $B$ are positive, so both triangles genuinely exist — the data given (two sides and a NON-included angle) do not determine the triangle uniquely.

questions.contextIntro: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 9$ cm, $BC = 7$ cm and the angle at $A$ measures $35^\circ$.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Find the probability that exactly $3$ customers arrive in a given $10$-minute interval.
parts.solution: Apply the Poisson formula with $\lambda = 2.5$ and $k = 3$:$$P(X = 3) = \frac{\mathrm{e}^{-2.5}(2.5)^{3}}{3!} = \frac{0.082085 \times 15.625}{6} = 0.21376\ldots$$ To three significant figures this is $0.214$.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find the probability that at least $3$ customers arrive in a given $10$-minute interval.
parts.solution: "At least $3$" is the complement of "at most $2$":$$P(X \ge 3) = 1 - P(X \le 2) = 1 - \left[P(0) + P(1) + P(2)\right].$$ Those three terms are $0.082085$, $0.205212$ and $0.256516$, summing to $0.543813\ldots$, so$$P(X \ge 3) = 0.456187\ldots \approx 0.456.$$ The boundary matters: $X \ge 3$ excludes $2$, so the complement stops at $2$.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Find the probability that exactly $4$ customers arrive in a given $20$-minute interval.
parts.solution: A Poisson mean scales with the length of the interval, so a $20$-minute window has $\lambda = 2 \times 2.5 = 5$. Then$$P(X = 4) = \frac{\mathrm{e}^{-5}(5)^{4}}{4!} = \frac{0.0067379 \times 625}{24} = 0.17547\ldots$$ So $0.175$ to three significant figures. Keeping $\lambda = 2.5$ here would be the error the question is testing.

questions.contextIntro: The number of customers arriving at a small shop follows a Poisson distribution with a mean of $2.5$ customers per $10$-minute interval.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Show that $g'(x) = x^{2}(3 - x)\mathrm{e}^{-x}$.
parts.solution: Apply the product rule with $u = x^{3}$ and $v = \mathrm{e}^{-x}$, so $u' = 3x^{2}$ and $v' = -\mathrm{e}^{-x}$:$$g'(x) = 3x^{2}\mathrm{e}^{-x} - x^{3}\mathrm{e}^{-x}.$$ Factoring out the common $x^{2}\mathrm{e}^{-x}$,$$g'(x) = x^{2}(3 - x)\mathrm{e}^{-x}.$$

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find the coordinates of the maximum point of the curve, giving the $y$-coordinate correct to three significant figures.

markscheme.note: $x = 0$ gives $g = 0$ and $g' $ does not change sign there, so the maximum is at $x = 3$

parts.solution: Since $\mathrm{e}^{-x} > 0$ always, the derivative vanishes when $x^{2}(3 - x) = 0$, that is at $x = 0$ or $x = 3$. At $x = 0$ the factor $x^{2}$ touches zero without changing sign, so the curve merely flattens; $g'$ is positive on both sides. At $x = 3$ the factor $(3 - x)$ changes from positive to negative, so that is a maximum:$$g(3) = 27\mathrm{e}^{-3} = 1.34425\ldots$$ The maximum point is $(3,\ 1.34)$.

questions.contextIntro: The function $g$ is defined by $g(x) = x^{3}\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ for $x \ge 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Find all real solutions of $h(x) = 0$, giving your answers correct to three significant figures.

markscheme.note: treat it as a quadratic in $x^{2}$, or solve on the GDC

parts.solution: The equation is a quadratic in $x^{2}$:$$\left(x^{2}\right)^{2} - 5x^{2} + 2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; x^{2} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{25 - 8}}{2} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}.$$ Both values are positive ($4.56155\ldots$ and $0.43844\ldots$), so each gives two real square roots:$$x = \pm 2.135779\ldots, \qquad x = \pm 0.662153\ldots$$ To three significant figures the four solutions are $\pm 2.14$ and $\pm 0.662$.

parts.label: b
parts.body: State the number of times the graph of $y = h(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis, and explain how the symmetry of $h$ accounts for the pattern of the solutions.

markscheme.note: $h(-x) = h(x)$, so the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis

parts.answer: four crossings; $h$ is even, so the roots pair up as $\pm$
parts.solution: Part (a) found four distinct real solutions, so the graph crosses the $x$-axis four times. The reason they pair up is the symmetry: every power of $x$ in $h$ is even, so$$h(-x) = (-x)^{4} - 5(-x)^{2} + 2 = x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 2 = h(x).$$ An even function has a graph symmetric about the $y$-axis, so whenever $x = a$ is a root so is $x = -a$ — exactly the $\pm$ pattern seen.

questions.contextIntro: The function $h$ is defined by $h(x) = x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 2$.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Explain why the first deposit grows to $2000(1.04)^{9}$ by the end of the tenth year.

markscheme.note: the first deposit is made at the end of year $1$
it then earns interest for the remaining $9$ years

parts.answer: it sits in the account for $9$ further years
parts.solution: The first $\$2000$ arrives at the END of year $1$, so it earns no interest during that first year. From then until the end of year $10$ there are $10 - 1 = 9$ complete years of compounding, each multiplying the balance by $1.04$. Hence that deposit is worth$$2000(1.04)^{9} = 2846.42\ldots$$ by the end of year $10$. The LAST deposit, by contrast, earns nothing and is still just $\$2000$.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find the total value of the account at the end of the tenth year, correct to the nearest dollar.

markscheme.note: the ten deposits form a geometric series

parts.solution: Each deposit has been compounding for a different number of years, so the ten amounts form a geometric series with first term $2000$ (the last deposit, uncompounded) and ratio $1.04$:$$S = 2000 + 2000(1.04) + \cdots + 2000(1.04)^{9}.$$ Summing with $S_n = \dfrac{u_1\left(r^{n} - 1\right)}{r - 1}$,$$S_{10} = \frac{2000\left((1.04)^{10} - 1\right)}{0.04} = 24012.21\ldots$$ To the nearest dollar the account holds $\$24{,}012$ — the $\$20{,}000$ deposited plus about $\$4{,}012$ of interest.

questions.contextIntro: At the end of each year for $10$ years, $\$2000$ is paid into an account that earns $4\%$ interest per year, compounded annually. Interest is added at the end of each subsequent year.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Find $C'(x)$.
parts.solution: Rewrite the middle term with a negative exponent so the power rule applies:$$C(x) = 0.5x + 200x^{-1} + 8.$$ Differentiating term by term,$$C'(x) = 0.5 - 200x^{-2} = 0.5 - \frac{200}{x^{2}}.$$

parts.label: b
parts.body: Show that the average cost is least when $x = 20$.
parts.solution: Set the derivative to zero:$$0.5 - \frac{200}{x^{2}} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; x^{2} = 400 \;\Rightarrow\; x = \pm 20.$$ The context requires $x > 0$, so $x = 20$. To confirm it is a minimum rather than a maximum, differentiate again:$$C''(x) = \frac{400}{x^{3}},$$ which is positive for every $x > 0$. The curve is concave up throughout, so the stationary point at $x = 20$ is the minimum.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Find the least average cost per unit.
parts.solution: Substitute the minimising value:$$C(20) = 0.5(20) + \frac{200}{20} + 8 = 10 + 10 + 8 = 28.$$ The least average cost is $\$28$ per unit, at a production level of $2000$ units.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Find the two production levels at which the average cost per unit is $\$33$.
parts.solution: Set the average cost equal to $33$ and clear the fraction by multiplying by $x$ (legal since $x > 0$):$$0.5x^{2} + 200 + 8x = 33x \;\Rightarrow\; 0.5x^{2} - 25x + 200 = 0.$$ Doubling,$$x^{2} - 50x + 400 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (x - 10)(x - 40) = 0,$$ so $x = 10$ or $x = 40$ — that is, $1000$ or $4000$ units. The two roots sit symmetrically either side of the minimum at $x = 20$ in the sense that both give the same cost, which is what the U-shape of the graph shows.

parts.label: e
parts.body: State, with a reason, what happens to the average cost per unit as $x$ becomes very large.

markscheme.note: so the average cost rises indefinitely — the fixed cost is spread thinner but the variable term dominates

parts.answer: it increases without bound, behaving like $0.5x + 8$
parts.solution: Look at the three terms separately as $x \to \infty$. The term $\dfrac{200}{x}$ represents the fixed cost spread over the output, and it tends to $0$. The constant $8$ stays put. The term $0.5x$ grows without limit, so$$C(x) \approx 0.5x + 8 \to \infty.$$ In context: producing more does spread the fixed cost thinner, which is what pulls the curve down for small $x$, but beyond $x = 20$ the rising per-unit term takes over and the average cost climbs indefinitely. The line $C = 0.5x + 8$ is an oblique asymptote.

questions.contextIntro: A factory's average cost per unit, in dollars, when $x$ hundred units are produced is modelled by $$C(x) = 0.5x + \frac{200}{x} + 8, \quad x > 0.$$ The diagram shows the graph of $C$ against $x$.

figure.alt_en: Graph of average cost C against x, falling to a minimum near x = 20 and then rising

parts.label: a
parts.body: Find the length of $BD$, correct to three significant figures.
parts.solution: Triangle $ABD$ has two sides and the included angle, so the cosine rule applies:$$BD^{2} = 40^{2} + 55^{2} - 2(40)(55)\cos 62^\circ = 4625 - 4400(0.469472\ldots).$$ That gives $BD^{2} = 2559.32\ldots$, so$$BD = 50.5898\ldots \approx 50.6\ \text{m}.$$

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find the area of triangle $ABD$, correct to three significant figures.
parts.solution: Use the included angle directly:$$\text{Area}_{ABD} = \tfrac{1}{2}(40)(55)\sin 62^\circ = 1100(0.882948\ldots) = 971.242\ldots$$ To three significant figures the area is $971$ m$^{2}$.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Find the size of the angle at $C$, correct to three significant figures.

markscheme.note: triangle $BCD$ now has all three sides known
rearranged cosine rule $\cos C = \dfrac{BC^{2} + CD^{2} - BD^{2}}{2(BC)(CD)}$

parts.solution: Once $BD$ is known, triangle $BCD$ has all three sides, so use the cosine rule rearranged for the angle:$$\cos C = \frac{BC^{2} + CD^{2} - BD^{2}}{2(BC)(CD)} = \frac{2025 + 1444 - 2559.32}{2(45)(38)}.$$ That is $\cos C = 0.265851\ldots$, so$$C = 74.5744\ldots^\circ \approx 74.6^\circ.$$ Carry the unrounded $BD$ into this step — rounding to $50.6$ first shifts the angle in the third figure.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Find the total area of the field, correct to three significant figures.
parts.solution: With the angle at $C$ known, the second triangle yields to the same area formula:$$\text{Area}_{BCD} = \tfrac{1}{2}(45)(38)\sin 74.5744^\circ = 855(0.963977\ldots) = 824.200\ldots$$ The diagonal splits the field into exactly these two triangles, so$$\text{Total} = 971.242 + 824.200 = 1795.44\ldots$$ To three significant figures the field covers $1800$ m$^{2}$.

parts.label: e
parts.body: A fence is to be built along the perimeter of the field. Find the total length of fencing needed.

markscheme.note: the perimeter is the sum of the four SIDES
the diagonal $BD$ is not part of the boundary

parts.solution: The boundary of the field consists of the four sides only — the diagonal $BD$ was a construction line used to solve the geometry, not a physical edge. So$$P = AB + BC + CD + DA = 40 + 45 + 38 + 55 = 178\ \text{m}.$$ Including $BD$ by mistake would add about $50.6$ m of fencing that is not needed.

questions.contextIntro: A field has the shape of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ shown in the diagram, with $AB = 40$ m, $AD = 55$ m, $BC = 45$ m and $CD = 38$ m. The angle at $A$ measures $62^\circ$. The diagonal $BD$ divides the field into two triangles.

figure.alt_en: Quadrilateral field ABCD with sides 40, 45, 38 and 55 metres, angle A of 62 degrees, and the diagonal BD drawn

parts.label: a
parts.body: Write down the two standard scores corresponding to the given percentages, each correct to three significant figures.

markscheme.note: inverse normal for the lower tail
inverse normal for the upper cut-off

parts.solution: Each percentage names a point of the STANDARD normal distribution. From the inverse normal,$$P(Z < z_1) = 0.10 \;\Rightarrow\; z_1 = -1.28155\ldots,$$$$P(Z < z_2) = 0.95 \;\Rightarrow\; z_2 = 1.64485\ldots$$ To three significant figures $z_1 = -1.28$ and $z_2 = 1.64$. The first is negative because $10\%$ is below the mean.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Write down two equations connecting $\mu$ and $\sigma$.
parts.solution: The standardising formula $z = \dfrac{t - \mu}{\sigma}$ rearranges to $t = \mu + z\sigma$. Applying it to each cut-off,$$42 = \mu + (-1.28155\ldots)\sigma,$$$$68 = \mu + (1.64485\ldots)\sigma.$$

parts.label: c
parts.body: Hence find $\mu$ and $\sigma$, each correct to three significant figures.
parts.solution: Subtracting the first equation from the second removes $\mu$:$$\left(1.64485 + 1.28155\right)\sigma = 68 - 42 \;\Rightarrow\; 2.92640\ldots\,\sigma = 26,$$ so$$\sigma = 8.88462\ldots$$ Substituting back into the second equation,$$\mu = 68 - 1.64485(8.88462\ldots) = 53.3861\ldots$$ To three significant figures $\mu = 53.4$ minutes and $\sigma = 8.88$ minutes.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Find the percentage of customers who stay longer than one hour, correct to three significant figures.

markscheme.note: standardise $t = 60$ with the values from part (c)

parts.solution: One hour is $60$ minutes. Standardising with the parameters found above,$$z = \frac{60 - 53.3861\ldots}{8.88462\ldots} = 0.744421\ldots$$ The upper-tail probability is$$P(T > 60) = P(Z > 0.7444\ldots) = 0.228311\ldots,$$ so about $22.8\%$ of customers stay longer than an hour. That sits sensibly between the given $5\%$ above $68$ minutes and the $50\%$ above the mean of $53.4$ minutes.

questions.contextIntro: The time $T$, in minutes, that customers spend in a restaurant is modelled by a normal distribution with unknown mean $\mu$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $10\%$ of customers stay less than $42$ minutes and $95\%$ stay less than $68$ minutes.
